1	\section{Experiments}

3	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
4	
5	We follow the self-training protocol described in \S\ref{sec:methodology}. All experiments use GPT2-125M on WikiText-103 with 500K tokens per generation, learning rate $5 \times 10^{-5}$, effective batch size 32, and 3 training epochs per generation. We run 8 generations (Gen~0--7) for each of the four data selection methods. All experiments are repeated across three random seeds (42, 123, 456), with each seed sharing the same Gen~0 checkpoint and generated data pools.
6	
7	For the model scaling experiment (\S\ref{sec:scale}), we additionally run GPT2-medium (355M parameters) under identical hyperparameters.
8	
9	Training is conducted on 2$\times$ RTX PRO 6000 (98GB total VRAM). A single 8-generation pipeline takes approximately 4 hours for GPT2-125M and 11 hours for GPT2-medium.
10	
11	\subsection{Main Results: Normal Cluster vs.\ RGDS Outlier}
12	\label{sec:main_results}
13	
14	Table~\ref{tab:gen7_summary} reports Gen~7 perplexity, rare n-gram ratio, and selection ratio across all methods and seeds. The central result is a stark bifurcation: three of the four methods cluster within a narrow perplexity band, while RGDS diverges catastrophically.

34	\end{table}

36	\paragraph{The normal cluster.} Random 50\%, External-only 50\%, and Uncurated 100\% occupy a PPL range of 41.75--50.28 across all completed seeds. A one-way ANOVA across the three methods yields $p \approx 0.20$, indicating no statistically significant difference within this group. This is itself a finding: whether one uses all the data, randomly subsamples half, or applies external-embedding selection to half, the collapse trajectory is statistically indistinguishable. The common factor is that none of these methods rely on the training model's own embeddings for selection.
37	
38	\paragraph{The RGDS outlier.} RGDS reaches Gen~7 PPL of 75.07 (seed=42) and 81.57 (seed=123), a \placeholder{+84\%} increase over the Random 50\% baseline (2-seed means: \placeholder{78.32} vs.\ 42.48). The effect size is massive (Cohen's $d \approx 10.3$), placing RGDS well outside the normal cluster by any conventional threshold. The effect is consistent across seeds: both available seeds show RGDS Gen~7 PPL exceeding every other method's Gen~7 PPL by at least 25 points.
39	
40	The magnitude of this gap warrants the term \textit{catastrophic acceleration}: RGDS does not merely fail to mitigate model collapse---it amplifies the degradation far beyond what occurs with no curation at all.
41	
42	\paragraph{Temporal dynamics.} Figure~\ref{fig:ppl_trajectory} plots PPL across generations. All methods begin at comparable Gen~0 perplexity ($\sim$37). Through Gen~3, trajectories overlap substantially. Divergence becomes visible at Gen~4, and by Gen~5--7, RGDS separates decisively. Uncurated and External-only both show a characteristic plateau-and-recovery pattern in the later generations (Uncurated: 56.25 $\rightarrow$ 50.28; External: 53.55 $\rightarrow$ 45.51 for seed=42), while RGDS monotonically degrades (53.82 $\rightarrow$ 75.07).
43	
44	\subsection{The Alignment Gap: Selection Ratio Analysis}
45	\label{sec:alignment_gap}
46	
47	The selection ratio (SR) reveals \textit{why} RGDS accelerates collapse. Recall that $\text{SR} > 1$ means the method preferentially retains samples rich in rare n-grams, while $\text{SR} < 1$ means it depletes them.
48	
49	\paragraph{RGDS ratio decay.} At Gen~0, RGDS begins with $\text{SR} = 1.04$ (seed=42) and $1.00$ (seed=123)---near parity, meaning the model's initial notion of ``diverse'' roughly aligns with content diversity. By Gen~7, the ratio has fallen to $0.52$ in both seeds. Figure~\ref{fig:ratio_trajectory} shows this is not a sudden collapse but a progressive drift: the ratio crosses the critical $\text{SR} = 1.0$ threshold at Gen~1 (seed=42: 0.91) and monotonically declines thereafter.
50	
51	The trajectory is remarkably consistent across seeds. Table~\ref{tab:sr_trajectory} reports the full RGDS ratio trajectory for seed=42:
52	
53	\begin{table}[t]
54	\centering
55	\small
56	\begin{tabular}{lcccccccc}
57	\toprule
58	\textbf{Gen} & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 & 7 \\
59	\midrule
60	SR & 1.04 & 0.91 & 0.93 & 0.94 & 0.90 & 0.81 & 0.72 & 0.52 \\
61	\bottomrule
62	\end{tabular}
63	\caption{RGDS selection ratio across generations (seed=42). The ratio falls below 1.0 by Gen~1 and reaches 0.52 by Gen~7, indicating the model's embedding space increasingly anti-correlates with content diversity.}
64	\label{tab:sr_trajectory}
65	\end{table}
66	
67	The interpretation is direct: by Gen~7, RGDS retains samples with only 52\% of the rare n-gram density of the full generated pool. What the model's embedding space considers ``maximally diverse'' is, in content terms, maximally homogeneous. This is the embedding alignment gap in action: the optimization target (embedding-space coverage) has diverged from the intended objective (content diversity), instantiating a Goodhart's Law failure \citep{goodhart1984problems}.
68	
69	\paragraph{External ratio stability.} In contrast, External-only maintains $\text{SR} > 1.0$ throughout all generations and seeds: seed=42 ranges from 1.10 to 1.28, seed=123 from 1.08 to 1.22, and seed=456 from 1.07 to 1.24 (Gen~7 mean $1.16 \pm 0.08$ across three seeds). The frozen Contriever encoder provides a stable diversity signal that does not degrade with the training model. This stability is the key differentiator: the selection \textit{algorithm} is identical between RGDS and External-only; only the embedding source differs.
70	
71	\paragraph{Random ratio.} Random selection yields $\text{SR} \approx 1.0$ by construction, confirming that it neither enriches nor depletes content diversity.

73	\subsection{Representation Quality Metrics Are Blind to Collapse}
74	\label{sec:blind_metrics}
75	
76	A natural question is whether standard embedding-quality diagnostics could detect the alignment gap in real time. We find they cannot.
77	
78	\paragraph{RankMe increases during collapse.} RankMe, which measures the effective dimensionality of the embedding space, rises from 280.32 at Gen~0 to 303.05 at Gen~3 for Uncurated seed=42 (+8.1\%). For RGDS seed=42, RankMe increases from 275.89 to 294.92 through Gen~4. By this metric, the embedding space \textit{improves} during the very period when RGDS begins its catastrophic divergence. The RGDS Gen~7 RankMe (292.72) remains higher than the Gen~0 value (275.89).
79	
80	\paragraph{$k$-NN probe accuracy remains stable.} The $k$-nearest-neighbor probe, which measures how well embeddings preserve categorical structure, maintains accuracy at 0.988 throughout the RGDS trajectory. The embedding space retains its ability to separate content categories even as its notion of ``diversity'' becomes decoupled from content diversity.

1	\section{Related Work}
2	
3	\subsection{Model Collapse in Iterative Training}
4	
5	\citet{shumailov2024ai} demonstrate that language models trained recursively on their own generated data undergo irreversible tail distribution erosion, establishing model collapse as a fundamental limitation of self-consuming training loops. \citet{alemohammad2024self} formalize this as Model Autophagy Disorder (MAD), proving theoretically that without fresh real data, iterative self-consumption degrades either quality or diversity. Subsequent work has extended these findings along several axes: \citet{dohmatob2025strong} establish a sharp phase transition in collapse behavior beyond a critical iteration threshold; \citet{seddik2024how} derive the maximum synthetic data proportion before collapse becomes inevitable; and \citet{guo2024curious} track the decay of lexical, syntactic, and semantic diversity across self-training generations, finding the strongest degradation in high-entropy generation tasks.
6	
7	On the mitigation side, \citet{gerstgrasser2024model} show that accumulating data across generations---rather than replacing it---can prevent collapse, while \citet{briesch2023large} confirm that replacement-based training degrades output diversity proportionally to synthetic data fraction. Our work operates within the replacement setting where collapse is expected, but reveals that a natural mitigation strategy---diversity-based data selection---can paradoxically \emph{accelerate} rather than prevent collapse when it relies on the training model's own representations.
8	
9	\subsection{Data Curation and Selection for LLM Training}
10	
11	Data selection has emerged as a key lever for training efficiency and quality. \citet{sorscher2022beyond} show that metric-guided data pruning can break neural scaling law power laws, motivating a family of embedding-based and model-aware selection methods. SemDeDup \citep{abbas2023semdedup} removes semantic near-duplicates using pretrained embeddings; D4 \citep{tirumala2023d4} combines deduplication with diversity-maximizing selection in embedding space; and DSIR \citep{xie2023data} selects data via importance resampling to match target domain feature distributions. More recent approaches optimize for task-specific signals: LESS \citep{xia2024less} selects instruction-tuning data based on gradient similarity to target tasks; DsDm \citep{engstrom2024dsdm} frames selection as datamodel-based optimization, noting that naive quality proxies can harm downstream performance; QuRating \citep{wettig2024qurating} uses LLM-generated quality scores; and SelectIT \citep{liu2024selectit} leverages model uncertainty for instruction data filtering.
12	
13	These methods are designed for one-shot curation of static datasets, where the embedding model is fixed and its representation quality is not in question. We show that the iterative self-training setting introduces a qualitatively different failure mode: when the model providing embeddings co-degrades with the training distribution, embedding-based selection amplifies rather than counteracts distributional collapse.
14	
15	\subsection{Embedding-Based Diversity and Representation Learning}
16	
17	Submodular maximization provides the algorithmic foundation for embedding-based diversity selection. \citet{iyer2013submodular} establish the optimization framework for submodular functions under budget constraints; \citet{wei2015submodularity} formalize data subset selection via facility location and graph-cut objectives in feature space; and \citet{mirzasoleiman2020coresets} apply gradient-embedding facility location for coreset construction. These methods assume a fixed, high-quality embedding space---an assumption we show breaks down under iterative self-training.
18	
19	Active learning methods face a related challenge: acquisition functions must remain well-calibrated as the model updates. BADGE \citep{ash2020deep} selects diverse batches via gradient embeddings; BatchBALD \citep{kirsch2019batchbald} maximizes joint mutual information; and subsequent work has shown that standard acquisition strategies degrade under distribution shift \citep{kothawade2021similar} and that embedding quality determines selection effectiveness \citep{yehuda2022active}. However, active learning typically involves a few rounds of model updating, not the sustained multi-generation feedback loop where selection bias compounds into the selecting model's own training data.
20	
21	The representation learning literature documents several mechanisms by which embedding spaces can lose expressiveness. \citet{jing2022understanding} characterize dimensional collapse in contrastive learning, where embeddings are driven into low-dimensional subspaces; \citet{hua2021feature} identify correlated feature axes as a driver of this collapse; and \citet{papyan2020prevalence} show that deep network representations converge to low-dimensional simplex structures during prolonged training. \citet{laurent2024feature} argue that feature collapse can be benign in classification, but our findings demonstrate that in iterative self-training, the same geometric contraction becomes pathological---it causes diversity selection to invert its intended effect.
22	
23	\subsection{Representation Drift and Proxy Misalignment}
24	
25	Our work connects two established literatures that, together, explain why internal-embedding diversity selection fails under iterative training.
26	
27	The concept drift literature studies how learned representations degrade under sustained distribution shift. \citet{lu2019learning} and \citet{gama2014survey} provide comprehensive taxonomies of drift detection and adaptation. In the continual learning setting, \citet{caccia2022new} quantify abrupt representation change during sequential training, and \citet{davari2022probing} demonstrate that representation-level forgetting proceeds independently of task performance---paralleling our finding that embedding geometry diverges from content diversity even as standard representation quality metrics (RankMe, $k$-NN accuracy) remain stable.
28	
29	The Goodhart's law and reward hacking literature formalizes the failure of proxy optimization under distribution shift. \citet{gao2023scaling} derive scaling laws showing that overoptimizing a proxy reward model degrades true objective performance; \citet{skalse2022defining} prove that non-trivial proxy rewards are inherently exploitable; \citet{pan2022effects} map how proxy-objective misalignment compounds under increasing optimization pressure; and \citet{karwowski2024goodhart} provide geometric characterizations of when proxy optimization diverges from the true objective. The embedding alignment gap is an instance of this phenomenon: internal embedding diversity serves as a proxy for content diversity, and this proxy progressively loses fidelity as the model's representations co-evolve with the selected data distribution.
30	
31	Finally, measuring diversity itself requires careful metric design. Distinct-N \citep{li2016diversity} and Self-BLEU \citep{zhu2018texygen} quantify surface-level lexical diversity, while \citet{tevet2021evaluating} audit failure modes of both n-gram and neural diversity metrics. MAUVE \citep{pillutla2021mauve} measures distributional gaps between generated and human text via embedding-space divergence frontiers. We use rare n-gram density as our content diversity measure precisely because, unlike embedding-based metrics, it is model-independent and directly captures the lexical tail erosion that defines model collapse.

26	\subsection{Connection to Concept Drift}
27	
28	The embedding alignment gap can be understood as a special case of concept drift \citep{lu2019learning, gama2014survey} in which the drift is endogenous: the model's own outputs define its future training distribution, which in turn reshapes its representations. In standard concept drift settings, the data distribution shifts due to external factors, and the model must adapt. In self-consuming training, the model \emph{causes} the distribution shift, creating a feedback loop where representation degradation and distributional shift co-amplify.

30	This endogenous drift is particularly insidious for embedding-based data selection because the selection mechanism relies on the very representations undergoing drift. Concept drift detection methods that monitor distributional divergence between training batches would flag the symptom (changing distributions) but not the cause (embedding-selection feedback). Addressing this failure mode requires either anchoring selection to a stable external reference---as External-only does---or monitoring the selection ratio to detect proxy inversion before it compounds.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

This work introduces the \emph{embedding alignment gap}---the progressive decorrelation between a model's internal embedding similarity and actual content diversity during iterative self-training---and demonstrates its consequences for embedding-based data curation. Through controlled self-training experiments with GPT2-125M over eight generations, we establish three principal findings.

First, the embedding alignment gap is real and self-reinforcing. The internal embedding diversity selection ratio declines from ${\sim}1.04$ at Generation~0 to ${\sim}0.52$ by Generation~7, indicating that the model's own embeddings increasingly select \emph{against} content-rich samples. Once the selection ratio crosses below~1.0, the proxy has inverted: diversity-maximizing selection over internal embeddings actively accelerates the loss of content diversity.

Second, this proxy inversion has catastrophic practical consequences. Representation-guided diversity selection (RGDS) using internal embeddings produces Generation~7 perplexity approximately 80\% higher than random baseline at the same 50\% data budget. Meanwhile, Random~50\% ($43.18 \pm 1.43$), External-only ($46.36 \pm 2.97$), and Uncurated ($47.04 \pm 2.90$) converge to a statistically indistinguishable cluster ($n{=}3$), confirming that the catastrophic degradation of RGDS is not an artifact of data reduction but a direct consequence of co-degrading embeddings.

Third, standard representation quality diagnostics fail to detect the alignment gap. Both RankMe effective dimensionality and $k$-NN probing accuracy remain stable throughout the collapse trajectory, rendering the proxy inversion invisible to conventional monitoring tools.

These findings carry several caveats. Our experiments are limited to GPT2-scale models, a single pretraining corpus, and a fixed self-training protocol; the generality of these results to larger models, diverse domains, and alternative training paradigms remains to be established (see the limitations and future directions discussed in \S\ref{sec:discussion}).

The practical implication is direct: internal embeddings that co-evolve with the training model should not serve as the selection criterion in iterative self-training pipelines. Random sampling---requiring no additional computation---provides a robust alternative that avoids proxy inversion entirely. When informed selection is desired, frozen external embeddings maintain alignment across generations. For practitioners who cannot abandon internal embeddings, the selection ratio offers a lightweight, real-time diagnostic: an overall declining trend below~1.0 signals that selection has begun to work against its intended objective, and corrective action---such as re-anchoring to an external encoder---should be taken before the degradation compounds.
